extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newspaper editors, media students, and media analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical principles for what newspapers consider 'news', how they gather and frame it, and what economic, legal, and organizational constraints shape coverage. Useful for evaluating or designing editorial policy and news-gathering practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metropolitan dailies as sources for general news
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively small set of metropolitan dailies (about 175 in cities over 100,000) constitute the press for 'general news' and make up the great press associations that exchange news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These key papers act not only for their own readers but as local reporters for other cities; rural and special presses largely take their general news from these metropolitan papers. Some metropolitan dailies and services are much richer and therefore disproportionately shape international and national reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic support from advertisers targeting prosperous urban publics
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic support for general news comes primarily from advertisers aiming at the fairly prosperous urban buying public whose purchases make newspaper advertising profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This buying public includes advertisers themselves and wields concentrated purchasing power; thus editorial impressions upon this group matter deeply and influence what papers choose to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty as a source of editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper that can really depend upon the loyalty of its readers is as independent as a newspaper can be, given modern economics of journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A devoted body of readers provides power greater than any individual advertiser and can break up advertiser pressure; when a paper betrays readers for an advertiser, it indicates either publisher sympathy with the advertiser or lack of confidence in reader support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers judge newspapers by treatment of matters within their experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of us tends to judge a newspaper, if we judge it at all, by its treatment of that part of the news in which we feel ourselves involved (our business, church, party, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local or personally relevant reporting that 'checks up' with readers' own experience immunizes a paper against criticism; most readers lack independent knowledge of distant events and therefore rely on how papers handle familiar matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal accountability limited to aggrieved parties
rubrics_metrics.description: General readers have no standing in law if they think they are being misled; only an aggrieved party can sue for slander or libel and must prove material injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal tradition treats general news as not a matter of common legal concern except where matters are immoral or seditious; this limits legal enforcement of general accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers accept stereotype-conforming news even if not accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: When news conforms to readers' stereotypes, they are less likely to challenge its truth; the 'canon of truth' cannot be applied in the same way to such items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News that fits preconceptions can be treated like fiction by readers; ideological or partisan presses are often judged differently because of this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversified non-political features to hold circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because political and social news interest the public intermittently, newspapers include many other features (society, scandal, sports, advice columns, comics, women's pages, recipes, etc.) primarily designed to hold a body of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors add varied content not because they are uninterested in public affairs but because they need dependable ways to maintain readership in a standardized news market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting is low-paid and lacks established professional corporate traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting is often the most poorly paid and least regarded branch of newspaper work; able men enter it temporarily to gain experience and then leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This economic situation inhibits formation of corporate traditions that raise admission standards, enforce codes, and create pride of craft—factors that would improve reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership/ideological control is not the sole explanation for press faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques that attribute all journalistic faults to 'Big Business' ownership ignore similar faults in anti-capitalist and other ideological presses; bias and unfairness are not unique to capitalist-owned papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid diagnosis must account for unfairness across different ownership/ideological types rather than assuming a single causal factor such as capitalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires an overt act or manifestation to be reported
rubrics_metrics.description: Before events become news they usually have to make themselves noticeable in some more or less overt act — e.g., bankruptcy filings, fires, arrests, votes, bills introduced, speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rumors, private conditions, or merely anticipated developments generally do not become publishable news until there is a definable, objectified occurrence or official record.

rubrics_metrics.name: The presence of record-keeping machinery increases certainty and newsability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is good machinery of record (stock tickers, election tabulating, vital statistics, customs records), news can be reported with precision and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more a happening can be fixed, objectified, measured and named, the more likely it is to be uncovered and reported as news; lack of such machinery makes reporting uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects lacking objective records tend to be debatable or neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics like states of mind, personalities, intentions, public opinion, working conditions, wage efficiency, unemployment, and other matters that are poorly recorded produce news that is debatable or is often neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such subjects do not 'take shape' as news until someone protests, investigates, or publicly creates an issue; reporters and readers often rely on stereotypes for these complex matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents filter and shape information for reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Much information is first filtered through publicity agents who present a formulated picture of situations—acting as censors and propagandists responsible to employers rather than to the whole truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reporters lack the time/resources to give a shape to many facts, organized groups employ press agents to supply ready-made narratives that suit their interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents create stunts/events to secure publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity men seeking free publicity often have to 'start something'—arrange a stunt or contrive an incident that will entangle their client with an event already newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful agitation (e.g., suffrage tactics) often depended on staging overt acts that made the cause continually visible in the routine news cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative reporting demands resources and is atypical for dailies
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations into deep social or industrial conditions require time, money, special talent, and extensive space; such work is beyond the routine resources of most daily newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough exposés and surveys (e.g., Pittsburgh Surveys) are costly and cannot be counted on as normal daily activities; daily papers therefore often cannot perform first-hand, extensive investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: News is usually an account of overt phases, not underlying causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine of the news reports the overt, stereotyped phases of situations (demands, strikes, disorder) rather than the complex underlying causes and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the readers' standpoint those overt phases are the most salient because they link to readers' immediate experience; consequently, reportage may neglect context and deeper issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists vary in ability to recognize nascent news
rubrics_metrics.description: There is wide divergence in judgment about when an event has a shape worthy of reporting; good journalists find news earlier and more often than hacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A skilled reporter may perceive signs and develop a story before an overt crisis; such anticipatory reporting is rare and distinguishes better reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press services standardize main events; scoops differentiate papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Press services tend to standardize reporting of main events across papers; only occasional great scoops or distinctive work make a paper indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because routine general news is similar across outlets, newspapers seek differentiation through exclusive reporting, specialty features, or editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of readers versus advertisers affects editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an axiom in newspaper publishing: 'more readers, more independence of the influence of advertisers; fewer readers and more dependence on the advertiser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A larger, stable readership dilutes the power of any single advertiser and allows greater editorial freedom; conversely, dependence on a small advertiser base increases advertiser influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local 'printed diary' function: chronicling familiar events retains readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A key function of a newspaper is to act as the 'printed diary of the home town'—recording local weddings, funerals, club meetings, prizes, and other items of familiar interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in large cities where general papers cannot fully serve this role, smaller local papers and special publications perform the diary function to secure reliable circulation among readers who want to see their lives reflected.
